title: Apple CEO Ternus Warns iPhone Duo Shortage Will Continue Indefinitely, Says No End Date】
body:
Apple’s flagship iPhone Duo remains in short supply, and the company’s chief operating officer John Ternus told Reuters there is no clear timetable for when production will catch up with demand. The admission came on the heels of Apple’s latest earnings release, where the tech giant highlighted robust sales across its product line but conceded that the Duo’s inventory constraints are likely to persist for the foreseeable future. Analysts say the shortage could have ripple effects on Apple’s revenue forecasts, supply‑chain partners, and consumer sentiment worldwide.

The iPhone Duo, launched earlier this year as a premium, dual‑camera device positioned to replace the older iPhone Pro Max series, has quickly become one of Apple’s most coveted models. Early adopters praised its advanced photography capabilities, larger display, and integration with Apple’s newest silicon. However, the device’s popularity has outstripped Apple’s ability to manufacture enough units, a problem compounded by ongoing semiconductor shortages, logistics bottlenecks, and the company’s decision to prioritize newer models such as the iPhone 16 series for production capacity. Ternus noted that “the Duo is constrained as of now, and we have no definitive end‑date for when we will fully satisfy the market demand.”

Supply‑chain experts point to a confluence of factors that have tightened Apple’s manufacturing pipeline. The global chip shortage, which began in 2020, continues to affect the availability of high‑performance processors required for the Duo’s A‑series chip. Additionally, the pandemic‑induced labor shortages at key contract manufacturers in Taiwan and China have slowed assembly lines. Apple’s own strategy of diversifying production to multiple sites—including a newly expanded facility in India—has helped mitigate some risks but also introduced complexities in quality control and logistics that can delay final shipments.

From a financial perspective, the shortage could shave billions off Apple’s quarterly earnings if the company cannot quickly ramp up output. While the iPhone segment still accounts for roughly half of Apple’s total revenue, the Duo’s premium pricing means each unit contributes a larger margin than standard models. Investors have already expressed concern, with Apple’s stock experiencing modest volatility since the earnings call. Nonetheless, analysts remain cautiously optimistic, noting that Apple’s services division—cloud, streaming, and app revenues—continues to grow and can partially offset hardware shortfalls. Moreover, the company’s deep cash reserves give it flexibility to invest in additional manufacturing capacity or secure more favorable component contracts.

Consumer reaction has been mixed. Some customers have opted to wait for the Duo’s next shipment, while others have turned to alternative Apple devices or even rival smartphones. In markets such as the United States, Europe, and China, resale prices for the Duo on secondary platforms have surged, reflecting the scarcity and fueling a nascent “gray‑market” dynamic. Retail partners have reported longer lead times and frequent back‑order notifications, prompting some to adjust their inventory strategies and prioritize other Apple models that are more readily available.

Looking ahead, Apple’s next steps will likely involve a combination of scaling up production lines, renegotiating component supply agreements, and possibly tweaking the Duo’s design to simplify assembly. The company’s upcoming product roadmap, which includes a rumored foldable device and further enhancements to its silicon line, could also reshape manufacturing priorities. For now, the iPhone Duo’s shortage serves as a reminder that even the world’s most efficient tech giant can be hamstrung by global supply constraints. Consumers and investors alike will be watching closely to see whether Apple can restore balance to its flagship lineup before the next fiscal quarter.
